title: What AI regulation could learn from the most hazardous industries in the world
headline: Applying high-reliability organisational theory to AI safety and governance
summary: The article argues that AI governance should move beyond one-off technical testing to adopt frameworks from high-hazard industries like aviation and nuclear energy. It suggests that normal accident theory and high-reliability theory offer models for managing complex, autonomous systems. The author emphasises that building a professional safety culture and robust assurance infrastructure is essential for managing the risks of frontier AI.
why_it_matters: For Australian organisations, this highlights that effective AI assurance requires moving beyond static compliance to embedding continuous monitoring, redundancy, and independent oversight into organisational culture.

quotes.text: This suggests that AI safety cannot be reduced to a model passing a one-off technical test before deployment. It must span different organisations and transcend international boundaries.
The institutional challenge is not simply to produce more AI regulation, but to create the professional safety culture that makes regulation meaningful.

classification.significance_reason: Provides a conceptual framework for evolving AI governance from simple compliance to high-reliability safety management.
